title: Synthetic Readers

spine.markdown: The system has undergone tuning and alpha testing by using synthetic (AI-powered) readers, which work through the text as human readers would, offering questions and comments. Each reader has been given their own profile. Such characterization of AI agents is a growing practice (Park et al. 2023; Argyle et al. 2023; Hämäläinen, Tavast, and Kunnari 2023; Masera 2026).

The Intertext system of characterization was derived from Freeman (2026). There are currently five profiles: general, collaborative, curious, skeptical, and student. The readers are powered by a different model (OpenAI GPT 5.6 terra), while the texts are generated by Claude Sonnet as noted above. The resultant readings (text and responses) may then be examined by a separate Claude agent and by the human author to evaluate the flow of the argument, the use of fund materials, links and graphics, and the quality of the prose.

These synthetic readers have shown that the model can absorb the argument of the text and apply it to new issues or examples raised by readers’ questions. The reader system has also helped the author to rethink the original argument and its evidence. For example, in The Digital Plenitude, some readers objected to the text’s formulation that traditional hierarchies in arts and culture have “almost, but not quite, vanished.” The system then drafted a more nuanced version. If this objection had occurred during a run with human readers, the spine or fund could have been changed for subsequent readers. The synthetic readings also suggested stylistic improvements to reduce the awkward wordings such as “the text claims.”

fundEntries.title: Why the reader comes from another company
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks why the synthetic readers use a different model from the text.
fundEntries.markdown: The text is written by Anthropic's Claude, while the synthetic reader is played by a model from OpenAI, so that the two roles are never one model in conversation with itself. The synthetic reader uses the same route into the system that a human reader's browser uses.

fundEntries.title: What the synthetic reader can see
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks whether the synthetic readers have access to the author's text or the instructions.
fundEntries.markdown: A synthetic reader sees what a human reader sees: the table of contents, the opening vignette of each section and the conversation so far. It never sees the instructions, the author's text or the fund. The titles and vignettes it reads are taken from the reader's page itself, so the synthetic reader cannot be given anything that the page does not show.

fundEntries.title: The five readers
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what the profiles are or how they differ.
fundEntries.markdown: The curious reader is a nonspecialist who follows closely and asks for clarification. The skeptical reader is an academic in a neighbouring field who notices unsupported claims and asks for evidence and counterexamples. The collaborative reader wants the work to be stronger and attends to its prose and movement. The general reader is the educated reader for whom the work is written, who reads for the argument. The student has the reading assigned and asks what terms mean, restating the argument to check it. Some profiles may search the web, but only occasionally and always naming what they found.

fundEntries.title: What a synthetic reader does each turn
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how a synthetic reader decides what to do, or what is recorded.
fundEntries.markdown: At each turn the synthetic reader chooses one action: to ask or comment, to press Return, to move to another section, or to finish. It also records a private reflection, rating its understanding, its confusion and its interest, with a sentence or two of explanation. These reflections are kept in the transcript and never sent to the text. The transcript also preserves the draft of each reply beside its revision.

fundEntries.title: How a round of readings is measured
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how the synthetic readings are evaluated, or what is counted.
fundEntries.markdown: Each round of readings is summarized in a report that counts the length of every reply and how often the limit is exceeded, the number of notes per reply, the replies in which the text speaks of its own argument, repeated phrases and closing sentences, the readers' private ratings, and how often the revision was applied. A separate count compares the replies' absolutes, hedges and closing formulas with the author's own prose. Such counts describe how the prose sounds; they do not show whether a claim is right.

fundEntries.title: The blind judge
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how one version of the system is compared with another.
fundEntries.markdown: To compare one version of the system with another, a separate Claude agent reads replies from several rounds, shuffled together and unlabelled, and answers the same questions about each without knowing which version produced it. A key kept apart from the judge then sorts the verdicts by round. The author reads the transcripts together with the judge's report and the counts, and decides what to change.

fundEntries.title: A loop for revising the work
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how the synthetic readings feed back into the text.
fundEntries.markdown: The synthetic readings serve as an editorial instrument as well as a test of the software. Comparable readings are run on the same edition and section; the transcripts and private reflections are read across the different profiles; an editorial hypothesis is formed rather than treating any single reply as a verdict; the author's text, the section boundaries, the opening vignettes or the instructions are revised as the evidence warrants; and the readings are run again. Synthetic readings never change the published text.

fundEntries.title: What synthetic readers cannot show
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks whether synthetic readers can stand in for people.
fundEntries.markdown: A synthetic reader argues on the text's own terms more than a human reader does, and it has no lived experience to bring to the reading. The synthetic readings reveal assumptions, overstatements, repetition and gaps. They cannot show how human readers will understand or respond, and they are no substitute for testing with human readers.

fundEntries.title: Experiments with the fund
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how the effect of the fund can be tested.
fundEntries.markdown: Two experimental editions, used only by the synthetic readers, give the text either the spine alone or the spine together with the fund, with web search turned off, so that the availability of the fund is the only difference between them. Comparing the two shows whether, and how, the text draws on optional material when it has it.
